comment.comment: Spec §Comment (fork v1.2): whole lines between `<!--` at the start of a line and `-->` followed only by blanks. Must be tried before #title, which would otherwise claim the opening line. An unterminated comment runs to the end of the file, as the spec requires.
comment.name: comment.block.xit markup.other.comment.xit

title.comment: Spec §Title: a single line that MUST NOT start with a blank character or `[`.
title.name: markup.underline.xit markup.other.task.title.xit

open-item.comment: Spec §Checkbox: exactly 3 characters, followed by a space or the end of the line. This is a begin/end rule rather than begin/while so that the context survives across continuation lines, which is what lets #due-date apply the "first due date only" rule to the whole description. The end is a zero-width match on the first line that does not continue the item: per spec §Description a continuation line is indented by exactly four spaces, and per spec §Item plus the glossary a line of only blank characters is blank and so ends the item, which is what the `(?=.*\S)` guard enforces. #due-date repeats this same end pattern so that the nested context pops together with its item.

closed-item.comment: Checked and obsolete items render their whole description as struck-through.

priority.comment: Spec §Priority: "any number of exclamation marks (`!`) and dots (`.`)", with the dots on one side only. Any number includes none, so `...` on its own is a priority with an importance of zero; the syntax guide shows it as one. Spec §Item allows additional space characters between the checkbox and the priority, so the separator is `[^\S\n]+` rather than a single space.

due-date.comment: Spec §Due Date: `-> ` followed by yyyy, yyyy-mm, yyyy-mm-dd, yyyy-Www or yyyy-Qq, with `-` or `/` as separator. The two lookbehinds are the left-hand boundary the syntax guide describes as "Due dates can be surrounded by a space or punctuation (apart from a hyphen or slash)": the first rejects a letter or digit before the arrow, so `Due-> 2022-01-31` is not a date, and the second rejects a hyphen or slash, so `---> 2022-01-31` is not one either. Both are negative, so a date at the very start of a description still matches. The backreference to group 5 forces one separator style per date. Trailing junk is rejected, but calendar validity beyond simple ranges cannot be checked here. This is a begin/end rule rather than a plain match so that the remainder of the item is tokenized without the due-date pattern: that is how "any additional due dates MUST be disregarded" is enforced. Its end is the end of the enclosing item, so the rule holds across continuation lines too.

tag.comment: Spec §Tag: the name is letters (Unicode L), digits, `_` or `-`. The `(?<=[\s\p{P}])` lookbehind is a deliberate divergence, and Discussion #51 is the thing to read before removing it: asked whether `a#tag` holds a tag, jotaen answered "Currently, yes", and named the consequences as accepted downsides (`bN144#y6Q!Jc` yields the tag `#y6Q`). The spec is silent on what may precede a `#`, so it agrees with him. His own xit-sublime rule carries this lookbehind regardless, so the reference implementation contradicts the answer, and it is the better behaviour. An unquoted value uses the same set; a quoted value may hold anything but its own quote, and an unterminated quote means the value is absent. The `=` is captured on its own, and the value after it is optional, because the spec says an empty tag value "MUST be treated the same as an absent tag value". So `#tag=` colours as one tag rather than leaving the `=` uncoloured in the middle of one, and `#tag="unterminated` colours as `#tag=` with the rest falling back to description. The `=` carries the tag scope but not the value scope: there is no value there to name.
